docs.text: We're still looking for teachers to share their experiences using live crayfish in the classroom! If you're an educator in the #GreatLakes region, you can reach out via the interest form here: purdue.ca1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_...

The ability for a single marbled crayfish to reproduce without needing a mate + the fact that they can produce up to 700 cloned offspring in a single reproductive cycle + their popularity in the pet trade = reason for concern that they could become invasive in the #GreatLakes region #25DaysofFishmas

Since being discovered in the 1990s, marbled crayfish have been introduced to several countries in Europe, as well as in Japan and Madagascar. While not established in the #GreatLakes yet, a marbled crayfish was found in 2021 in Burlington, Ontario only a few miles from Lake Ontario #25DaysofFishmas

Out now! Our new curriculum for grades 6-12 helps educators across the #GreatLakes region engage their students to think critically about freshwater ecosystems through the lens of crayfish - read more about it here: iiseagrant.org/new-crayfish...

Teachers! IL-IN Sea Grant is looking to understand the use of live crayfish in classroom settings. If you are (or know) a science teacher in grades 3-12 in the #GreatLakes region who has used live crayfish in the classroom, we'd like to chat! Interest form: purdue.ca1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_...

Get your copy of the new Great Lakes Almanac to Invasive Crayfish! For each #crayfish species, a detailed description and illustration is provided highlighting significant physical features that can be used to identify the ##invasivespecies. www.canr.msu.edu/resources/gr...
In just a handful of decades, the rusty crayfish has become dominant in the Great Lakes. WTTW News reporter Patty Wetli takes us on a deep dive into this elusive invader. to.wttw.com/4gWsN2R

So what happens if marbled crayfish become invasive in the #GreatLakes? They could outcompete native crayfish species due to their faster growing rates + aggressive behavior. They may also have negative impacts on the fishing industry as they've done in other places like Madagascar #25DaysofFishmas
A crayfish making his way back into Lake Superior this morning

Not all claws are created equal - meet the invasive crayfish crew of Michigan. 📣 Check out our Great Lakes Almanac to Invasive Crayfish and learn how to tell these invaders apart from our friendlier native crawdads. 👉 bit.ly/crayfishalma...

The non-native virile crayfish (Faxonius virilis) in particular has boomed in regions of the western US without any native crayfishes like the Colorado River (nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/Fact...). Given its abundance in irrigated lands, I wonder if we're missing damages and costs as an ag pest?

1/ A 🧵 on some recent research by our lab on invasive crayfish: Sheppard et al (2024) found that projected climate warming in the Great Lakes will reduce the maximum feeding rate & increase the frequency & duration of gravid states of marbled crayfish. Read: redpath-staff.mcgill.ca/ricciardi/Sh...
Crayfish monitoring training events are being held across the Great Lakes region this fall. Free to attend! docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1F...

This past fall, I located two distinct crayfish on the shore of Lake Michigan. iNaturalist offered several suggestions, so I went down a path of of reading papers and studies about native and invasive crayfish of the Great Lakes, learning about spots, pincers, and carapace distinctions.
These are crayfish that live in Lake Michigan. I believe these ones are rusty crayfish, which is considered an invasive species in the Great Lakes.
Pleased to have delivered a seminar on invasive crayfish to the MNR Lake Ontario Management Unit at the historic Glenora research station.

The Great Lakes Almanac to Invasive Crayfish highlights four invaders: Rusty Crayfish (Faxonius rusticus), Red Swamp Crayfish (Procambarus clarkii), Marbled Crayfish (Procambarus virginalis), and Australian crayfish (Cherax species).

Hemimysis - the bloody red shrimp- was first detected in 2006 in the Great Lakes and is now found in all 5 lakes. Its latest global distribution is part of this new publication led by .bsky.social. neobiota.pensoft.net/article/1440...

Researcher Donn Branstrator authored a study on the first evidence of bloody red shrimp 🦐 (BRS) establishing in Lake Superior. BRS is an adaptable, omnivorous invader that can alter food webs by competing with native species and reshaping energy pathways. Check it out: doi.org/10.1016/j.jg...

Taking beach combing to the next level. Count me among the lucky to have seen the Rusty Crayfish, Lake Michigan invader extraordinaire. Read my interview w/Prof. Reuben Keller, an expert on these creatures. news.wttw.com/2025/02/27/h...
